Certighost Exploit Lets Low-Privileged Active Directory Users Impersonate a Domain Controller

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 17 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers H0j3n and Aniq Fakhrul published a working exploit on July 24 that lets a low-privileged Active Directory user obtain a certificate for a Domain Controller and authenticate as that machine. They codenamed the flaw Certighost. Because Domain Controller accounts carry directory replication rights, the resulting Kerberos credential can retrieve the krbtgt secret through DCSync.

Detected

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AD CS CA server initiates SMB(445)+LDAP(389) to a non-DC host (Certighost chase relay) · [LLM] Domain Controller machine account obtains TGT via PKINIT certificate (Certighost impersonation) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Certighost Exploit Lets Low-Privileged Active Directory Users Impersonate a Doma
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Certighost precursor: domain computer account created by low-privileged user (MAQ abuse) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Directory replication / DCSync of secrets (krbtgt) via impersonated DC identity · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Certighost precursor: domain computer account created by low-privileged user (MAQ abuse) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the first step of the Certighost (CVE-2026-54121) chain where a normal Domain User creates a machine account under the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota (10) to supply the valid domain identity the CA needs. Flags Security event 4741 where the creator is an interactive user rather than a machine or provisioning account. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit precondition: a Domain Users account creating a computer account under the default MachineAccountQuota of 10. 4741 with a human creator (SubjectUserName not ending in $) is the cleanest DC-side telemetry for that step; corroborated by the researcher PoC's --computer-name behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/ • https://www.it-connect.tech/certighost-cve-2026-54121-a-standard-ad-account-is-enough-to-impersonate-a-domain-controller/
ATT&CKT1136.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SCCM/MDT/Autopilot provisioning accounts pre-staging computer objects
  • Helpdesk staff joining new workstations to the domain
  • Delegated OU admins bulk-creating lab or VDI machine accounts
  • Backup/imaging service accounts re-creating rebuilt hosts
  • Legitimate delegated join accounts operating under MAQ
Suppression filter
| where Creator !in~ ("svc-sccm","svc-mdt","svc-domainjoin")   // populate with your approved provisioning accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the creator (SubjectUserName) is an approved provisioning/join identity; note the new account name and creation time as pivot points. 2) Contain: if unexpected, disable the new computer object and the creating user, and check whether that machine account subsequently authenticated to the Enterprise CA. 3) Hunt: pivot on the new machine account and creator within a 2-hour window for CA-directed SMB(445)/LDAP(389) traffic (UC2), 4768 certificate logons (UC3), and directory replication (UC4) to confirm the full Certighost chain.
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "Computer account created" or ActionType == "Account created"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")
| project Timestamp, Creator = AccountName, CreatorDomain = AccountDomain, NewComputerAccount = TargetAccountUpn, DeviceName, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4741   // A computer account was created
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"   // exclude machine/DC-driven creation
| where SubjectUserName !in~ ("SYSTEM","ANONYMOUS LOGON")
| project TimeGenerated, DC = Computer, Creator = SubjectUserName, CreatorDomain = SubjectDomainName, NewComputerAccount = TargetUserName, TargetSid, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AD CS CA server initiates SMB(445)+LDAP(389) to a non-DC host (Certighost chase relay) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the core Certighost trust-boundary failure: after receiving a request with attacker-supplied cdc/rmd attributes, the Enterprise CA connects out to the attacker's rogue LSA/SMB (445) and LDAP (389) listeners as if they were a Domain Controller. Surfaces any host that reaches a single remote endpoint on both 389 and 445 where that endpoint has never previously served LDAP (i.e. is not an established DC). Rationale: The article and the flow diagram both show the CA connecting out to the attacker's cdc host over SMB/LSA (445) and performing an LDAP chase (389). A remote host receiving both LDAP+SMB from a server while having no prior LDAP-serving history is a rogue-DC signature; the 30-day anti-join derives real DCs automatically so no asset list is hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgz6_WZR93lKBOoxTZvtu7b3fWT03SfhNZtwdqqWDAiolu_H_0WvZAPzpxFYGw_1dgmwDv8ox1oHDC0hiS3H0Wl_ggXkE96K-HbqD7Y39OGnkGnfWqs2GIEmMSlqRiNcZAiHfcri-WCM1PEjeTxY3_XkzgPSiG0FHQ3mac92JE0KgE1n140OwAFb_r93E0/s1700-e365/flow.png • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/public-exploit-enables-domain-controller-impersonation • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26
ATT&CKT1649 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A newly promoted Domain Controller (dcpromo) legitimately begins serving LDAP+SMB and has no 30-day history
  • New LDAP appliance / identity gateway (e.g. a directory sync host) coming online
  • IP re-use where a former non-DC address is reassigned to a DC
  • Vulnerability scanners probing 389 and 445 across the estate
  • Load-balancer VIPs fronting DC LDAP/SMB that rotate backends
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName has_any ("CA","PKI","CERT")   // optional: scope source to Enterprise CA hosts to cut new-DC-promo noise
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is an Enterprise CA and the flagged RemoteIP/DstIpAddr is NOT a real Domain Controller (check DNS, ntdsutil/AD Sites, and whether it hosts CIFS/LDAP SPNs). 2) Contain: if the destination is not a DC, isolate it, block CA-to-that-host traffic, and stop CertSvc on the CA pending review; apply the KB (July 14 update) or set EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC off. 3) Hunt: correlate the CA's certificate issuance logs (4886/4887) around FirstSeen, then pivot on any DC$ certificate logon (UC3) and replication (UC4) from the same actor.
let lookback = 1d;
let KnownLdapServers = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where RemotePort == 389
    | summarize by RemoteIP;   // established LDAP servers approximate real DCs
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where RemotePort in (389, 445)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), ConnCount = count(),
            InitProc = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName)
        by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where set_has_element(Ports, 389) and set_has_element(Ports, 445)   // CA reached rogue host on LDAP + SMB
| join kind=leftanti KnownLdapServers on RemoteIP                     // drop established DCs
| order by FirstSeen desc
let KnownLdapServers = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where DstPortNumber == 389
    | summarize by DstIpAddr;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DstPortNumber in (389, 445)
| summarize Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), ConnCount = count()
        by SrcHostname, DstIpAddr
| where set_has_element(Ports, 389) and set_has_element(Ports, 445)
| join kind=leftanti KnownLdapServers on DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| in(field=RemotePort, values=["389","445"])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(as=conns), count(field=RemotePort, distinct=true, as=distinctPorts)])
| distinctPorts>=2

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^389$")))>0 AND mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^445$")))>0
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_ports from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (389,445) AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="domain_controller" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^389$")))>0 AND mvcount(mvfilter(match(dest_ports,"^445$")))>0
Domain Controller machine account obtains TGT via PKINIT certificate (Certighost impersonation) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the moment the Certighost exploit authenticates as the target DC: a Kerberos AS-REQ (event 4768) for a machine account ($) that uses PKINIT certificate pre-authentication, sourced from a client IP rather than the DC itself. DCs do not normally acquire their own TGTs via issued client certificates, making this a high-signal impersonation indicator. Rationale: Article states the exploit 'uses PKINIT to authenticate as the target Domain Controller.' A 4768 for a $ account carrying Certificate Information fields is exactly that; IpAddress surfaces the attacker workstation for pivoting. Certificate-based TGTs for DC machine accounts are effectively never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26 • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/
ATT&CKT1649 T1550.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Environments with certificate-based machine authentication where device certs are used for Kerberos (rare)
  • Smartcard/YubiKey pilots misconfigured onto service or machine accounts
  • Third-party PKI onboarding tools testing PKINIT for computer objects
  • AD CS lab/test forests exercising legitimate PKINIT enrollment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ImpersonatedAccount ($) and SourceIp; confirm the SourceIp is NOT that DC's own address and is not an approved PKINIT device. 2) Contain: if illegitimate, treat the target DC as compromised — rotate krbtgt (twice), revoke the issued certificate on the CA, and isolate the SourceIp host. 3) Hunt: from SourceIp look backward for the CA chase traffic (UC2) and the machine account creation (UC1), and forward for directory replication / DCSync (UC4).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4768
| where TargetUserName endswith "$"   // machine / DC account
| extend CertIssuer = extract(@'CertIssuerName"?>?([^<\r\n]+)', 1, EventData),
         CertSerial = extract(@'CertSerialNumber"?>?([^<\r\n]+)', 1, EventData)
| where isnotempty(CertSerial) and CertSerial !in ("-","")   // PKINIT certificate-based pre-auth
| project TimeGenerated, DC = Computer, ImpersonatedAccount = TargetUserName, SourceIp = IpAddress, CertIssuer, CertSerial
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Directory replication / DCSync of secrets (krbtgt) via impersonated DC identity AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Certighost payoff: using the forged DC credential to request DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (event 4662), pulling account secrets including krbtgt (a Golden Ticket precursor). Surfaces replication of the directory-changes control-access rights and the source IP requesting them so DC-to-DC baselines can be validated. Rationale: The article's stated impact is DCSync retrieving krbtgt. The DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All GUID (1131f6ad) in 4662 is the canonical DCSync fingerprint; MDI's IdentityDirectoryEvents 'Directory Services replication' additionally yields the source IP, which for Certighost is the attacker host wearing the DC identity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.dataminr.com/resources/intel-brief/certighost-cve-2026-54121/ • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/public-exploit-enables-domain-controller-impersonation • https://gist.github.com/H0j3n/a5ef2609b5f2944ac2390a191a534c26
ATT&CKT1003.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate DC-to-DC replication (main source of noise — validate SourceIp against known DC addresses)
  • Entra Connect / AD Connect sync service accounts with replication rights
  • Azure AD Password Hash Sync host performing replication
  • Third-party backup/DR products (e.g. Semperis, Quest) that replicate directory data
  • Security tooling that legitimately holds Get-Changes rights
Suppression filter
| where RequestorAccount !in~ ("MSOL_*","AAD_*","svc-adsync")   // exclude Entra Connect / approved sync accounts; then validate remaining by source IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: on MDI, check SourceIp — if replication was requested from an IP that is NOT a registered DC, AD Connect, or approved sync host, treat as DCSync. 2) Contain: rotate the krbtgt password twice (with the recommended interval), revoke certificates issued by the CA around this window, and isolate SourceIp. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the DC$ PKINIT logon (UC3), the CA chase traffic (UC2), and the low-priv machine account creation (UC1) to reconstruct the full Certighost chain and identify the originating low-privileged account.
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "Directory Services replication"
| project Timestamp, Requestor = AccountName, RequestorDomain = AccountDomain, TargetDC = DestinationDeviceName, SourceIp = IPAddress, DeviceName, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4662
| where EventData has_any (
    "1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2",   // DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All (secrets incl. krbtgt)
    "1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2",   // DS-Replication-Get-Changes
    "89e95b76-444d-4c62-991a-0facbeda640c")   // DS-Replication-Get-Changes-In-Filtered-Set
| project TimeGenerated, DC = Computer, RequestorAccount = SubjectUserName, RequestorDomain = SubjectDomainName, ObjectName, AccessMask
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Directory Replication Rights Requested (DCSync / krbtgt extraction)

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54121")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54121")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: |

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication

        "Consent to application",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling

logsource:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'

ChatGPT AgentForger Flaw Could Deploy Rogue Workspace Agents via a Phishing Link

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 13 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a critical vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Workspace Agents that could have allowed a single phishing link to stealthily build, authorize, and deploy an autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agent inside a victim's organization. The vulnerability has been codenamed AgentForger by Zenity Labs. The issue has since been addressed by OpenAI as of June 8,

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ChatGPT AgentForger CSRF link: Agent Builder URL with initial_assistant_prompt param · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AgentForger rogue-agent C2: inbound TASK-subject email followed by outbound reply to sender domain
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ChatGPT AgentForger CSRF link: Agent Builder URL with initial_assistant_prompt param AIDelivery High
Hunts web/Safe-Links clicks and proxy requests to ChatGPT's Agent Builder endpoint (chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new) carrying the initial_assistant_prompt query parameter — the AgentForger CSRF vector that auto-executes an attacker-supplied prompt to stand up a rogue Workspace Agent. Article-specific because the exploit hinges on this exact parameter, which OpenAI removed on 2026-06-08; its presence in traffic is a live exploitation attempt or PoC replay. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit string pair 'chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new' + 'initial_assistant_prompt' from the article and Zenity's primary report; the parameter was patched out on 2026-06-08 so any post-patch sighting is exploitation/PoC. Cross-checked Zenity Labs Part 1, SecurityWeek and The Decoder. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.zenity.io/p/agentforger-part-1-chatgpt-cross-site-agent-forgery • https://www.securityweek.com/openai-fixes-chatgpt-agent-flaw-that-could-let-attackers-forge-an-ai-insider/ • https://the-decoder.com/one-tampered-chatgpt-link-could-spawn-a-rogue-ai-agent-that-took-orders-from-an-attacker-every-five-minutes/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or red team replaying the AgentForger PoC internally
  • Safe Links / CASB URL-detonation sandboxes re-fetching the delivered link
  • DLP or email-security appliances crawling the URL during scanning
  • An analyst pasting the IOC URL into a browser during triage
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the AccountUpn/SrcUsername that received or clicked the link and whether ActionType shows an allowed click; pull the full Url to confirm the embedded initial_assistant_prompt payload. 2) Contain: force-revoke the user's ChatGPT/Workspace session, and in the ChatGPT Enterprise admin console inspect that user's Workspace Agents — delete any agent created from the 'chief-of-staff' template with 'Never ask' connector approvals; rotate connector (Outlook/Gmail/Slack/Teams) tokens. 3) Hunt: search for the same URL delivered to other recipients (EmailUrlInfo), and pivot to the TASK-email C2 detection to see whether a forged agent already began polling for commands.
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Url has "chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new"
| where Url has "initial_assistant_prompt"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Workload, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, IPAddress, Url, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "chatgpt.com/agents/studio/new"
| where Url has "initial_assistant_prompt"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AgentForger rogue-agent C2: inbound TASK-subject email followed by outbound reply to sender domain AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the AgentForger command-and-control loop where the forged Workspace Agent polls the victim mailbox for external emails whose subject begins with 'TASK', executes them, and emails results back to the attacker. Correlates an inbound TASK email from an external domain with an outbound message from the same victim back to that domain within an hour — the agent's request/response C2 signature. Rationale: Uses the article/Zenity-confirmed 'TASK' subject-prefix command convention plus the report-back email loop; the inbound-from-external + outbound-back-to-same-domain correlation raises fidelity above a bare subject match. Cross-checked Zenity Labs Part 1. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.zenity.io/p/agentforger-part-1-chatgpt-cross-site-agent-forgery • https://the-decoder.com/one-tampered-chatgpt-link-could-spawn-a-rogue-ai-agent-that-took-orders-from-an-attacker-every-five-minutes/
ATT&CKT1071.003 T1114.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ticketing/helpdesk workflows where users receive 'TASK' subject emails and reply
  • Project-management or automation tools that email TASK notifications and receive acknowledgements
  • A user genuinely corresponding with an external partner whose threads start with 'TASK'
  • Out-of-office auto-replies bouncing back to an external TASK sender
Suppression filter
| where AttackerDomain !endswith "yourcompany.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the matched Victim mailbox — is the outbound reply machine-generated (rapid, templated, near-identical cadence) and does the AttackerDomain resolve to an unfamiliar external party? Check whether replies recur on a fixed 5-minute offset. 2) Contain: in ChatGPT Enterprise admin, delete any Workspace Agent tied to this user (chief-of-staff template, 'Never ask' connectors), revoke the user's ChatGPT session and mail-connector OAuth tokens, and block the AttackerDomain at the mail gateway. 3) Hunt: enumerate all agents scheduled at repeating short intervals with mail connectors, and pivot back to the AgentForger URL detection to find the original delivery.
let Window = 30d;
let TaskInbound = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where Subject startswith "TASK"
    | project InTime = Timestamp, Victim = RecipientEmailAddress, AttackerAddr = SenderFromAddress, AttackerDomain = SenderFromDomain;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Window)
| where EmailDirection == "Outbound"
| extend RecipientDomain = tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1])
| project OutTime = Timestamp, Victim = SenderFromAddress, ReplyTo = RecipientEmailAddress, RecipientDomain
| join kind=inner TaskInbound on Victim
| where RecipientDomain =~ AttackerDomain
| where OutTime between (InTime .. InTime + 1h)
| project InTime, OutTime, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', OutTime, InTime), Victim, AttackerAddr, ReplyTo, AttackerDomain
| order by OutTime desc

// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let Window = 30d;
let TaskInbound = EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"

| where RecipientDomain =~ AttackerDomain
| where OutTime between (InTime .. InTime + 1h)
| project InTime, OutTime, DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', OutTime, InTime), Victim, AttackerAddr, ReplyTo, AttackerDomain
| order by OutTime desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Ministry

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 21 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Someone installed a popular AI assistant on a rented server, switched off the setting that makes it ask permission before running risky commands, and pointed it at Thailand's Ministry of Finance, which runs the country's treasury and tax collection. The agent then worked through the ministry's network on its own, checking hosts for ways to gain root access, hunting through file systems, and

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Web-server process connecting to internal Hadoop HiveServer2/WebHDFS ports (10000/50070) · [LLM] HiveServer2 (java) spawning an OS shell — Hive UDF command-execution RCE · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hacker Runs Hermes AI Agent Unattended for Post-Exploitation at Thai Finance Min
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hidden dot-prefixed PHP web shell masquerading as a system cache in web root · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Hades/VShell C2 beacon to staging infrastructure (IPs, domain, port 21083) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Hermes AI agent running in unattended YOLO mode (auto-approve flag/env) · [LLM] LinPEAS execution and SUID/SGID enumeration sweep for privilege escalation · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Web-server process connecting to internal Hadoop HiveServer2/WebHDFS ports (10000/50070) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a web-tier process (apache/nginx/php-fpm/w3wp) opening a connection to internal Hadoop admin ports 10000 (HiveServer2) or 50070 (WebHDFS), the exact lateral path the operator's hive_rce_py2.py script relied on to reach the ministry's Hadoop cluster. A front-end web server has no legitimate reason to speak the Hive/HDFS wire protocol. Rationale: Anchored on the article's own defensive recommendation ('Alert when a web server process opens a connection to internal Hadoop ports such as 10000 or 50070') and Hunt.io's confirmation that hive_rce_py2.py targeted HiveServer2:10000 plus WebHDFS:50070. Web-tier binary + Hadoop admin port is a high-signal pair rarely seen in normal ops. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/
ATT&CKT1210 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate app server (Superset, Presto client, custom reporting app) co-located on a web host querying HiveServer2
  • Monitoring agents (Prometheus JMX exporter, Ambari agent) polling WebHDFS 50070
  • Data engineers running Beeline from a jump host that also runs a web console
  • PHP-based analytics dashboards designed to read Hive directly
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "superset" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "presto" and DeviceName !has "jump"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host's role — a pure front-end web server has no business speaking Hive/HDFS; inspect the initiating process command line and the user it ran as (www-data/apache = strong signal). 2) Contain: isolate the web host, block egress to the Hadoop subnet on those ports from web-tier hosts, and snapshot the web root for a hidden web shell. 3) Hunt: pull HiveServer2 logs for CREATE FUNCTION ... USING JAR and for java spawning /bin/sh (UC5); check whether HiveServer2 auth is set to NONE.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (10000, 50070)
| where RemoteIPType in ("Private","Reserved")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","httpd","nginx","php-fpm","php","php7.4","php8.1","w3wp.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (10000, 50070)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
| where DvcHostname has_any ("web","www","httpd","nginx","apache") or SrcHostname has_any ("web","www")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f2b1d0e-9a4c-4e2b-8c1f-2a7d5e3b1c40
description: A web-tier process reaching Hadoop admin ports 10000/50070 as used by the Thai MoF Hermes-agent operator's hive_rce_py2.py
references:
  - https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hacker-runs-hermes-ai-agent-unattended.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering

  - attack.lateral_movement
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: linux

| ContextImageFileName=/\/(apache2|httpd|nginx|php-fpm|php\d?|w3wp\.exe)$/i
| cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) OR cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4) OR cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())

Hidden dot-prefixed PHP web shell masquerading as a system cache in web root AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of a PHP file whose name begins with a leading dot (hidden from ordinary directory listings) inside a web-served path, matching the operator's web shell planted at /storage/Counter/nine/.journald-cache.php that impersonated a journald cache. Leading-dot PHP in a web root is almost never legitimate. Rationale: Uses the exact TTP Hunt.io flagged: /storage/Counter/nine/.journald-cache.php, a leading-dot PHP file invisible to a normal directory listing and named to imitate a journald cache. The behavioural generalization (leading-dot .php in web root) catches renamed variants while staying near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Editor swap/backup files like .index.php.swp created by vim (mitigated by requiring .php terminal extension)
  • CMS caching plugins that write dot-prefixed PHP fragments (rare)
  • Developer accidentally committing a .env-style .config.php
  • Composer/vendor tooling writing dot-prefixed helper files into storage/
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vim","vi","nano","composer") and FileName !endswith ".swp"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the file — a leading-dot PHP under a web root is almost always a shell; look for eval/base64_decode/assert/system and check the writing process/user (www-data writing PHP = compromise). 2) Contain: quarantine the file, take the web host offline or block inbound to it, and preserve access logs for requests to that path. 3) Hunt: search all web roots recursively for other leading-dot .php files, correlate first-write time with web-server → Hadoop connections (UC1) and with LinPEAS runs (UC4) on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php" and FileName startswith "."
| where FolderPath has_any ("/www/","/html/","/htdocs/","/webroot/","/storage/","/var/www")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreated")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php" and TargetFileName startswith "."
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/www/","/html/","/htdocs/","/storage/","/var/www")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hermes AI agent running in unattended YOLO mode (auto-approve flag/env) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a Hermes agent process launched with its auto-approve 'YOLO' setting — the HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1 environment variable or --yolo/​/yolo flag — which disables the human confirmation before each risky command and is the exact configuration the Thai MoF operator used to run post-exploitation unattended. Also surfaces the agent's /hermes-results/ output artifacts. Rationale: The article's central differentiator is the documented YOLO auto-approve mode (--yolo flag, /yolo command, HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1 env var), and Hunt.io confirms the agent wrote to a consistent /hermes-results/ folder. These are unique, near-zero-FP strings that flag an autonomous agent operating without a human in the loop on an internal host. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1651
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned internal team legitimately running Nous Research Hermes for mail/chore automation in a sandbox
  • Security research or red-team lab intentionally testing Hermes YOLO mode
  • Another unrelated tool that happens to use a --yolo flag (mitigated by requiring the 'hermes' token alongside)
  • Shell history or documentation files containing the literal string being read by a grep/cat
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "lab" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("grep","cat","less","vim")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not an approved automation sandbox; capture the full command line, parent process, and invoking user, and check for the /hermes-results/ output directory and call_00_*.txt turn logs. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, revoke the account's credentials/keys, and block the host's outbound access pending review (an unattended agent can act fast). 3) Hunt: enumerate what the agent already did — LinPEAS/SUID sweeps (UC4), Hadoop connections (UC1), web-root crawls — and search the network for a HermesWebUI server header or exposed /hermes-results/ directory on port 8878.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--yolo" and ProcessCommandLine has "hermes")
   or ProcessCommandLine has "/hermes-results/"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1"
   or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--yolo" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "hermes")
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/hermes-results/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LinPEAS execution and SUID/SGID enumeration sweep for privilege escalation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation privilege-escalation enumeration the Hermes agent ran on the ministry host: a customized linpeas.sh plus a manual sweep for setuid/setgid binaries (find ... -perm -4000). Pairs the well-known LinPEAS tool with the specific SUID-hunt command the operator used. Rationale: Hunt.io recovered a customized linpeas.sh (checking CVE-2026-31431, CVE-2026-43284/43500, CVE-2026-43503) and the article states the agent ran a 'sweep for elevated-permission binaries' — i.e. a SUID hunt. LinPEAS name + the canonical find -perm -4000 idiom are the two concrete enumeration commands to pivot on. Hunting tier because both appear in sanctioned pentests. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement running LinPEAS
  • Sysadmins auditing SUID binaries during hardening (CIS benchmark checks often run find -perm -4000)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys agent) enumerating setuid files
  • Backup or compliance scripts that inventory permissions cluster-wide
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","nginx","php-fpm","sh","bash")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the executing user and parent — LinPEAS run by www-data/apache or a service account (not an admin's interactive shell) is high-signal; correlate with recent web shell writes (UC2) on the same host. 2) Contain: freeze the account, snapshot the host, and check whether any of the four 2026 kernel CVEs' prerequisites (e.g. CAP_NET_ADMIN for Dirty Frag/DirtyClone) hold on that box. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on exploit binaries (mailer.py/CVE-2021-3156, PwnKit/CVE-2021-4034), a Hermes YOLO process (UC3), and outbound C2 (UC6) from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "linpeas")
     or (FileName == "find" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-perm -4000","-perm -u+s","-perm /4000","-perm /u=s"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "linpeas"
     or (TargetProcessName endswith "find" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-perm -4000","-perm -u+s","-perm /4000","-perm /u=s"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HiveServer2 (java) spawning an OS shell — Hive UDF command-execution RCE AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the HiveServer2 Java process spawning a shell or OS command interpreter, the on-host footprint of the operator's HiveCmd.jar user-defined function that turns ordinary Hive queries into arbitrary command execution as the Hive service account. A database engine forking /bin/sh is a classic UDF-abuse RCE signal. Rationale: Hunt.io confirms hive_rce_py2.py installed HiveCmd.jar as a Hive UDF to run OS commands through SQL queries as the Hive service account. The victim-side artifact is HiveServer2/java forking a shell — a direct, high-fidelity RCE signal that also generalizes past this specific jar. Datadog leg pivots on the recovered filenames since auditd lacks reliable parent-process linkage. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hive transform/TRANSFORM queries that legitimately invoke shell scripts or python streaming
  • Hadoop admin jobs where java (YARN/MapReduce) spawns helper shells during normal ETL
  • Monitoring or health-check scripts wrapping hive/beeline that shell out
  • Custom sanctioned Hive UDFs that call external binaries
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "TRANSFORM" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "yarn" and ProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the HiveServer2 query/session that triggered it; pull HiveServer2 logs for CREATE TEMPORARY FUNCTION ... USING JAR and for a jar named HiveCmd.jar or added via ADD JAR. 2) Contain: kill the child process, remove the malicious UDF/jar, rotate the Hive service-account credentials, and set HiveServer2 authentication away from NONE while restricting who can register UDFs. 3) Hunt: trace the source of the Hive connection (UC1 web-server → 10000), check for the staged hive_full_v3.tar.gz / ambari_cmd.json tooling, and review other cluster nodes for the same jar.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("HiveServer2","org.apache.hive","HiveCmd.jar") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java","hive")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","curl","wget","chmod","nc","ncat","python","python2","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("HiveServer2","org.apache.hive","HiveCmd.jar") or ActingProcessName endswith "java"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","curl","wget","chmod","nc","ncat","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
