Hades/VShell C2 beacon to staging infrastructure (IPs, domain, port 21083) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host callbacks to the operator's confirmed command-and-control and staging infrastructure: four Hong Kong/Malaysia IPs, the redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com domain, and the VShell listener on TCP 21083. Also anchors on the Hades Go implant and VShell stage payload hashes for host-side confirmation. Rationale: Hunt.io's IOC table (second source beyond The Hacker News, also reported by BleepingComputer/SecurityAffairs) lists these four IPs, the redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com domain, VShell on TCP 21083, and SHA-256 hashes for the Hades Linux/Windows implants and VShell stages. Direct-IOC alerting on confirmed C2 infrastructure is high-confidence and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/thailand-ministry-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hermes-ai-agent-used-to-automate-attack-on-thai-finance-ministry/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195941/hacking/thailands-ministry-of-finance-targeted-with-hermes-ai-agent-running-unattended-hades-implant-staged.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or research infrastructure scanning/sinkholing the same IPs (benign, but investigate)
  • Shared hosting: one of the Hong Kong ASNs later reassigned to a legitimate service on the same IP
  • Security tooling (VirusTotal retro-hunt, honeypot) deliberately connecting to the IOC
  • An analyst's sandbox detonating the sample and beaconing out
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vt-scanner","nmap","masscan") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a masquerading name (kworker, multipathd, accounts-daemon, dwm_33b7.exe, ctfmon) beaconing to these IPs is Hades/VShell; hash the binary and compare to the published SHA-256s (e.g. d252ee7b34…c7d1e2 Hades Linux, 0f8c905a…85f2fc VShell Linux stage 1). 2) Contain: block the four IPs, port 21083, and sinkhole redhatupdating432.dnsrd.com; isolate the beaconing host and kill the implant. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the implant hashes and the Hades HTTP beacon URIs (/assets/app.min.js, /assets/vendor.js, /assets/main.js with UA 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36'), and review how the implant was staged (web shell UC2 / Hive RCE UC5).

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["0f8c905aa25c86f85454acb7e77bf5c50220c2a82e5b69a33741e55c8a85f2fc", "a9447ae174f4aa54f760b7d7cc985c1a970f31e151d3ff66fac247f99ba1b509", "ec7e9ab43a0cc65d29f0b84a93ba88c43d01fed3dec5c968525dc73c03cbfda2", "b65b7ede835ebba36294d52d7780065523340ee09bb8b209ef2dc495e53dfd53", "d252ee7b348b7e43e432d8fb154465838f5cd5fb564905323460e6f0a0c7d1e2", "c74010aa82e8164c8d4ca9e073ec6b9a762e53db67498b22f5ccaef3a82853f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Golden Chickens Resurfaces With Four New Malware Families and Modular Implants

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 18 use cases 9 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actors behind the Golden Chickens malware-as-a-service (MaaS) ecosystem have resurfaced with four new malware families, indicating that the operators are showing no signs of stopping despite extensive public disclosures into their inner workings. The malware families in question are: TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken, a modularized variant of ChonkyChicken, and a modified web browser credential

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Golden Chickens TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken OCX side-load via regsvr32 from user-writable paths · [LLM] TAG-195 WinComCtl Run-key persistence pointing to staged OCX · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Golden Chickens WebSocket C2 from regsvr32/rundll32 to non-standard port 3000 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ChonkyChicken browser session hijack via Chrome/Edge remote-debugging (CDP) off-screen · [LLM] ChromEggscalator ABE-bypass debug log and OCX staging artifacts · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Golden Chickens TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken OCX side-load via regsvr32 from user-writable paths AIInstallation High
Hunts regsvr32.exe registering an .ocx payload from %TEMP%/%LOCALAPPDATA%/Downloads/Packages, which is TAG-195's shared delivery model for TinyEgg, ChonkyChicken and ChromEggscalator (updater.ocx, mscomctl.ocx, chromelevator.ocx, mscom.ocx via /i, DllInstall or DllRegisterServer). Article-specific because it pins the LOLBin+extension+location+filename set the campaign reuses across all four families. Rationale: Anchored on RF's finding that all four families are packaged as OCX and launched with regsvr32 + filename-gating on updater.ocx/mscomctl.ocx/chromelevator.ocx/mscom.ocx from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages and %TEMP%; regsvr32 registering an .ocx from a user profile is near-zero in benign fleets. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chonkychicken-steals-chrome-credentials/ • https://gbhackers.com/four-modular-malware-families/
ATT&CKT1218.010 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ActiveX/OCX installers run from a user Downloads folder during app deployment
  • Developer or QA registering a self-built .ocx from a build output dir under AppData
  • Software packaging tools (SCCM/Intune) staging OCX controls in Temp before registration
  • Legacy line-of-business apps that ship mscomctl.ocx and self-register on first run
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","msiexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full regsvr32 command line and parent process; confirm the OCX path is user-writable and hash the .ocx (VT/RF lookup). Check for the WinComCtl Run key on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the regsvr32 process tree, quarantine the .ocx, and block the staging domain/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same OCX filenames, for Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port, and for outbound WebSocket to port 3000.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "regsvr32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".ocx"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("updater.ocx","mscomctl.ocx","chromelevator.ocx","mscom.ocx")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Packages\") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/i","/s","DllInstall","DllRegisterServer"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".ocx"
| where CommandLine has_any ("updater.ocx","mscomctl.ocx","chromelevator.ocx","mscom.ocx")
   or (CommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Packages\") and CommandLine has_any ("/i","/s","DllInstall","DllRegisterServer"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Golden Chickens OCX Side-Load via Regsvr32 from User-Writable Path
id: 8f2b1c40-3d5e-4a91-9f0a-1c2d3e4f5a6b
description: Detects regsvr32 registering a Golden Chickens (TAG-195) OCX payload from a user-writable directory
references:
  - https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/golden-chickens-resurfaces-with-four.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1218.010
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith: '\regsvr32.exe'
  selection_named:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'updater.ocx'
      - 'mscomctl.ocx'
      - 'chromelevator.ocx'
      - 'mscom.ocx'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains: '.ocx'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Packages\'
  condition: selection_img and (selection_named or selection_path)
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\REGSVR32.EXE) @CommandLine:(*.ocx* OR *.OCX*) (@CommandLine:(*updater.ocx* OR *mscomctl.ocx* OR *chromelevator.ocx* OR *mscom.ocx*) OR @CommandLine:(*\\Temp\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Downloads\\* OR *\\Packages\\*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/regsvr32\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\.ocx/i
| CommandLine=/(updater\.ocx|mscomctl\.ocx|chromelevator\.ocx|mscom\.ocx|\\(Temp|AppData|Downloads|Packages)\\)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=regsvr32.exe (Processes.process="*updater.ocx*" OR Processes.process="*mscomctl.ocx*" OR Processes.process="*chromelevator.ocx*" OR Processes.process="*mscom.ocx*" OR (Processes.process="*.ocx*" AND (Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search NOT user="*$"
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=regsvr32.exe (Processes.process="*updater.ocx*" OR Processes.process="*mscomctl.ocx*" OR Processes.process="*chromelevator.ocx*" OR Processes.process="*mscom.ocx*" OR (Processes.process="*.ocx*" AND (Processes.process="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process="*\\Packages\\*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

TAG-195 WinComCtl Run-key persistence pointing to staged OCX AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the HKCU ...\CurrentVersion\Run value named WinComCtl (or any Run value pointing to a regsvr32-invoked .ocx under Packages/AppData), the shared persistence approach across TinyEgg and ChonkyChicken. Registry pivot distinct from the process-creation UC. Rationale: RF documents the exact value name (WinComCtl) under HKCU Run pointing at the staged OCX in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages; the value-name string plus .ocx autostart data is a high-fidelity, campaign-unique persistence artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://cyberpress.org/golden-chickens-unleashes-tinyegg/
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche app legitimately auto-starting a registered OCX control via a Run value
  • IT deployment scripts writing Run keys that call regsvr32 for a required control
  • Software using the generic value name 'WinComCtl' for a real Common Controls dependency (rare)
  • Backup/restore tooling recreating a previously-existing Run value
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files\" or RegistryValueData has @"\Windows\System32\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump RegistryValueData to get the exact OCX path + regsvr32 args; correlate with the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) and check whether that OCX exists on disk. 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the Run value, quarantine the referenced OCX, and capture it for analysis before deletion. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process across the fleet and look for regsvr32-OCX executions and port-3000 WebSocket C2 from the same hosts.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "WinComCtl"
   or (RegistryValueData has ".ocx" and RegistryValueData has_any ("regsvr32", @"\Packages\", @"\AppData\Local\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValue =~ "WinComCtl"
   or (RegistryValueData has ".ocx" and RegistryValueData has_any ("regsvr32", @"\Packages\", @"\AppData\Local\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

ChonkyChicken browser session hijack via Chrome/Edge remote-debugging (CDP) off-screen AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Chrome/Edge/Brave launched with --remote-debugging-port and the tell-tale off-screen --window-position=-32000,-32000 (and/or a non-browser parent supplying --user-data-dir), which is how ChonkyChicken drives live browser sessions over Chrome DevTools Protocol for credential and session theft. Distinct process-tree pivot. Rationale: RF details ChonkyChicken launching Chrome/Edge with --remote-debugging-port=9222, --user-data-dir and --window-position=-32000,-32000 driving a local 127.0.0.1:9222 CDP endpoint; the off-screen window flag plus remote-debugging is a textbook covert-CDP signal with negligible benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://cybersecuritynews.com/chonkychicken-steals-chrome-credentials/ • https://www.cryptika.com/chonkychicken-malware-steals-chrome-credentials-moves-laterally-and-spies-on-victims/
ATT&CKT1185 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser test frameworks (Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright) launching Chrome with --remote-debugging-port on QA hosts
  • RPA bots driving a headless browser for legitimate automation
  • Developers debugging web apps with remote debugging enabled
  • Kiosk/monitoring software that positions a browser off-screen
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","chromedriver.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", @"\selenium\", @"\ci\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process of the browser launch — a non-browser parent (regsvr32/rundll32/unknown) with --remote-debugging-port is high-confidence malicious; confirm no CI/RPA tooling on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, terminate the browser + parent tree, and force-reset the user's browser-backed credentials and session tokens. 3) Hunt: check the same host for regsvr32-OCX execution, WinComCtl Run key, xlog.txt in ProgramData, and port-3000 WebSocket C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--window-position=-32000"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\brave.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where CommandLine has "--window-position=-32000"
   or (CommandLine has "--user-data-dir" and not(ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Golden Chickens WebSocket C2 from regsvr32/rundll32 to non-standard port 3000 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections initiated by regsvr32.exe/rundll32.exe (the processes hosting the OCX implants) to public IPs on the non-standard WebSocket C2 port 3000, plus the campaign's known C2 IPs/domains. A LOLBin making an internet WebSocket connection is the TinyEgg/ChonkyChicken beacon shape. Rationale: RF reports the WebSocket C2 uses non-standard port 3000 with endpoint /ws/agent and lists C2 IPs (65.20.102.161/105.177, 108.61.209.100) and domains (xtrafftrck.net, thessa.trackgrid.net); pairing that with the OCX-host process (regsvr32/rundll32) reaching a public IP is near-zero benign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://gbhackers.com/four-modular-malware-families/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internal dev service listening on port 3000 (Node.js default) reached by a legitimately signed tool — but rarely by regsvr32
  • Rundll32 hosting a legitimate control that phones a vendor endpoint on a high port
  • Proxy/PAC rewrites that make regsvr32 traffic appear to hit an unexpected port
  • Security tooling that proxies EDR telemetry over 3000
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIPType == "Private")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating regsvr32/rundll32 command line references an .ocx and resolve the remote IP/domain reputation (RF/VT). 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the C2 IPs/domains and port 3000 egress at the perimeter, and kill the OCX host process. 3) Hunt: reverse the join — find all hosts talking to the same C2 IPs, then check each for the WinComCtl Run key and OCX side-loads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort == 3000
   or RemoteIP in ("65.20.102.161","65.20.105.177","108.61.209.100","70.34.205.43")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("xtrafftrck.net","trackgrid.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where DstPortNumber == 3000
   or DstIpAddr in ("65.20.102.161","65.20.105.177","108.61.209.100","70.34.205.43")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url

ChromEggscalator ABE-bypass debug log and OCX staging artifacts AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects file creation of ChromEggscalator's operational artifacts — xlog.txt under C:\ProgramData (browser-discovery/extraction debug log), lg.txt under %TEMP% (execution-gating log), and staged mscom.ocx/chromelevator.ocx in %TEMP% — used when ChonkyChicken drops the Chrome App-Bound-Encryption bypass helper to steal browser credentials. File-event pivot on the credential-theft stage. Rationale: RF names ChromEggscalator's debug log C:\ProgramData\xlog.txt and ChonkyChicken's %TEMP%\lg.txt plus the staged helper %TEMP%\mscom.ocx (aka chromelevator.ocx) written before chrome_extract; the specific filename+path set on the ABE-bypass helper is article-unique though single-file names carry some benign-name risk (hence medium confidence). Cross-checked against: • https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/tag-195-evolves-maas-ecosystem • https://github.com/xaitax/Chrome-App-Bound-Encryption-Decryption • https://www.techradar.com/pro/security/google-chrome-cookie-encryption-system-can-be-easily-bypassed-experts-warn
ATT&CKT1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated application writing a generic 'lg.txt' or 'xlog.txt' log file to Temp/ProgramData
  • Legitimate software staging a real mscomctl-style OCX in Temp during install
  • Backup/AV products writing xlog.txt-style logs under ProgramData
  • A developer's own logging harness emitting lg.txt during testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".ocx"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that created the artifact (InitiatingProcessFileName) and check for adjacent regsvr32-OCX execution and a %TEMP%\output\ directory of extracted credentials. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the OCX + logs (preserve for IR), and force-reset all browser-stored credentials and session cookies for the logged-on user. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same artifacts fleet-wide and correlate with CDP browser launches and port-3000 C2 on those hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where (FileName =~ "xlog.txt" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (FileName =~ "lg.txt" and FolderPath has @"\Temp\")
   or (FileName in~ ("mscom.ocx","chromelevator.ocx") and FolderPath has @"\Temp\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFileName =~ "xlog.txt" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\")
   or (TargetFileName =~ "lg.txt" and TargetFilePath has @"\Temp\")
   or (TargetFileName in~ ("mscom.ocx","chromelevator.ocx") and TargetFilePath has @"\Temp\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

NodeBB Patches Eight AI-Found Flaws Exposing Admin Access and Private Chats

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 16 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Eight security flaws in NodeBB went public on Wednesday, along with the code to exploit them. Aikido Security rates all eight as high severity and says its AI pentest agents found them in a six-hour review of the forum software's source code. Every version before 4.14.0 is affected. NodeBB has fixed them all, and administrators should be on 4.14.2. The simplest one takes a settings change. A

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] NodeBB federation actor spoofing (CVE-2026-58593): external POST to ActivityPub inbox · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NodeBB privilege escalation: non-admin reaching /api/admin/* after homePageCustom bypass · [LLM] NodeBB i18n translation-token XSS: [[topic:merged-message,...]] injected in request URI · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NodeBB unauthenticated private-data enumeration via ActivityPub outbox / message endpoints · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
NodeBB privilege escalation: non-admin reaching /api/admin/* after homePageCustom bypass AIExploitation Medium
Hunts NodeBB's client-side-only admin block bypass (pre-4.14.0), where a regular member points the homePageCustom setting at /admin and then loads admin-only routes. Surfaces HTTP 200 responses on /admin and /api/admin/* (error log, user CSV export, logo upload, category management) so an analyst can confirm whether the requesting account/IP is actually an administrator. Rationale: Uses the exact admin routes the Aikido writeup names as reachable via the homePageCustom client-side bypass (/api/admin/advanced/errors, /api/admin/users/csv, /api/admin/uploadlogo). Hunting tier because web access logs lack the requester's forum role, so the analyst confirms non-admin identity. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch empty: no inbound HTTP-request path telemetry exists in those sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/eight-nodebb-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate forum administrator using the admin dashboard
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring probing /admin health endpoints
  • CI/CD or plugin health checks hitting /api/admin/*
  • Backup jobs pulling /api/admin/users/csv on schedule
Suppression filter
| where CsUsername !in ("admin", "nodebb-admin") and CIp !in ("10.0.0.0/8")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve CIp/CsUsername to a forum account and confirm whether it holds an admin/global-moderator role; a member or unauthenticated session reaching /api/admin/* = true positive. 2) Contain: force-logout the account, reset its session/token, and confirm NodeBB is upgraded to 4.14.2 (client-side-only block is fixed server-side there). 3) Hunt: review that source IP for prior PUT /api/v3/users/*/settings changing homePageCustom to /admin, and for logo/category/user-export changes made under the bypass.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem == "/admin" or CsUriStem startswith "/admin/" or CsUriStem startswith "/api/admin/"
| where ScStatus in (200, 201)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Paths=make_set(CsUriStem, 25), Methods=make_set(CsMethod, 5) by CIp, UserAgent, CsUsername
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: NodeBB admin panel / admin API access (privilege-escalation bypass)
id: 8f3b1e2a-6c4d-4f9a-9b1e-2a7c5d8e0f11

NodeBB i18n translation-token XSS: [[topic:merged-message,...]] injected in request URI AIExploitation High
Hunts NodeBB's second-pass translation XSS (pre-4.14.0, the 325-file rebuild in 4.14.0). User input containing NodeBB translator tokens ([[ / %5B%5B / topic:merged-message) is smuggled into a page and executed on the translation pass. Flags requests whose URL or query string carries these translator markers, including the /flags?quick= reflected sink. Rationale: NodeBB's translator uses the [[namespace:key,args]] syntax; the writeup's PoC is literally /flags?quick=]][[topic:merged-message,javascript:alert(origin). Matching [[ / %5B%5B / topic:merged-message in the URI is a precise attack signature with near-zero legitimate use in query strings. contains (not has) is used deliberately — the bracket sequences are not token-aligned. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cyberpress.org/nodebb-patches-eight-high-severity-flaws/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/QA testing i18n rendering with literal [[ tokens
  • Security scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nuclei) probing for XSS with bracket payloads
  • Legitimate deep links that happen to contain double square brackets in a parameter
  • Translation plugin admin previewing a translation key
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has_any ("nuclei", "zap", "burp", "nikto") and CsUsername !in ("qa", "i18n-admin")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode CsUriQuery and check for a translator key chained to a script sink (javascript:, onerror, alert(origin)); confirm ScStatus 200 (payload reflected/stored). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, purge any forum post/flag containing the token, and verify upgrade to 4.14.2 which rebuilt the translation pass. 3) Hunt: search post bodies and /flags?quick=, /topic, and profile fields for stored [[ tokens; review UrlClickEvents/proxy logs for victims who loaded the injected page.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriQuery contains "[[" or CsUriQuery contains "%5B%5B" or CsUriQuery contains "topic:merged-message" or CsUriStem contains "[[" or CsUriStem contains "%5B%5B"
| project TimeGenerated, CIp, CsMethod, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, ScStatus, UserAgent, CsUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NodeBB federation actor spoofing (CVE-2026-58593): external POST to ActivityPub inbox AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound ActivityPub delivery abused by CVE-2026-58593 and the Aikido federation flaws, where a remote server posts to a NodeBB inbox and NodeBB fails to bind attributedTo to the authenticated actor, letting an outside server author posts/DMs as any local uid (including admin). Surfaces external POSTs to /category/*/inbox, /uid/*/inbox and /ap/inbox/* so rare/new peer instances can be reviewed. Rationale: CVE-2026-58593 (CVSS 8.7, corroborated on NVD) lets a remote actor set attributedTo to a bare uid (e.g. 1 = admin) on objects posted to the inbox routes the Aikido writeup enumerates (/category/*/inbox, /uid/*/inbox, /ap/inbox/*). Access logs rarely capture the JSON body, so this baselines external inbox POSTs by peer; new/rare source IPs are the pivot. Requires federation enabled. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58593 • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Mastodon/ActivityPub peer instances delivering to your inbox
  • Relay servers fanning out activities to category inboxes
  • Federation load/health checks from a known partner instance
  • Your own forum's outbound-then-inbound reply threads
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the source IP, pull the inbox POST body from WAF/app logs (if captured) and check whether attributedTo/object.actor matches the HTTP-Signature keyId actor; a mismatch (e.g. attributedTo: 1) = spoofing. 2) Contain: defederate/block the offending instance domain and IP, disable federation if not required, and upgrade to 4.14.2. 3) Hunt: review recent posts/DMs authored by admin or high-privilege uids for content that arrived via federation, and correlate against unknown peer domains in /.well-known/webfinger and /ap/actor/* lookups.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem endswith "/inbox" and (CsUriStem startswith "/category/" or CsUriStem startswith "/uid/" or CsUriStem startswith "/ap/inbox/")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Posts=count(), Endpoints=make_set(CsUriStem, 25) by CIp, UserAgent
| order by FirstSeen desc

NodeBB unauthenticated private-data enumeration via ActivityPub outbox / message endpoints AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the two no-account NodeBB flaws that leak private data: reading private messages one-at-a-time (/message/:mid) and dumping private-category contents (/category/:cid/outbox) to any requester. Flags a single client fetching many distinct message/outbox objects — the enumeration pattern the article describes ('one at a time'). Rationale: Targets the exact endpoints the writeup names for the unauthenticated private-message read (/message/:mid) and private-category disclosure (/category/:cid/outbox). The >5 distinct-object threshold captures the 'one at a time' enumeration while a single legitimate fetch won't trip it. Sigma omitted: this is an aggregation/threshold rule, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/eight-high-severity-vulnerabilities-nodebb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/eight-nodebb-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ActivityPub peers pulling public category outboxes
  • Search-engine or archive crawlers walking message/topic URLs
  • A logged-in power user legitimately reading many of their own DMs
  • Internal migration/export tooling iterating over objects
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has_any ("Mastodon", "friendica", "bot", "crawler", "spider")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP/UA is unauthenticated (no valid session) and that the fetched /message/ or /category/*/outbox objects belong to private conversations/categories; volume of distinct IDs indicates scraping. 2) Contain: block the IP at the WAF, rotate any secrets exposed in leaked DMs, and upgrade to 4.14.2 which adds the missing authorization checks on the side routes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same IP/UA for /.well-known/webfinger, /ap/actor/* and /uid/*/inbox activity indicating a full federation-based recon-and-read chain.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| where CsUriStem startswith "/message/" or (CsUriStem startswith "/category/" and CsUriStem endswith "/outbox")
| summarize DistinctObjects=dcount(CsUriStem), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Objects=make_set(CsUriStem, 50) by CIp, UserAgent
| where DistinctObjects > 5
| order by DistinctObjects desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as hits, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_objects, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.uri_path) as sample_paths from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="GET" (Web.uri_path="/message/*" OR Web.uri_path="/category/*/outbox") by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_objects > 5
| sort - distinct_objects
| tstats summariesonly=false count as hits, dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_objects, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.uri_path) as sample_paths from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method="GET" (Web.uri_path="/message/*" OR Web.uri_path="/category/*/outbox") by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
