Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

Kimi K3 Agents Found Redis Zero-Days and Built RCE Exploit, Researchers Say

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 13 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Redis shipped seven security releases on July 23 after researchers published authenticated RCE PoCs for stock Redis 6.2.22, 7.4.9, 8.6.4, and 8.8.0. All four chains require RESTORE. The Streams chains also need EVAL and XGROUP; the 8.8.0 chain needs EVAL and the bundled RedisBloom module. Redis says the underlying memory flaws may lead to remote code execution. redis-server process spawns a shell/interpreter (RESTORE-chain system() RCE payoff) AIExploitation High
Hunts the terminal step common to all four published Redis RCE chains (6.2.22/7.4.9/8.6.4 Streams shared-NACK and 8.8.0 RedisBloom TDigest): after corrupting memory via RESTORE the exploit poisons a hash function so a crafted GET/command invokes system(), making the redis-server daemon the parent of /bin/sh or another interpreter. A production Redis server never legitimately forks a shell, so this is a near-zero-FP signal of successful exploitation. Rationale: Every chain in the article and PoC repo converges on invoking system() from redis-server, so redis-server parenting a shell is the highest-fidelity observable. Parent=redis-server + child interpreter is the article-specific pivot, not a generic shell-spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/berabuddies/redis-poc • https://redis.io/blog/security-advisory-cve202623479-cve202625243-cve-2026-25588-cve202625589-cve-2026-23631/ • https://securityonline.info/redis-rce-vulnerabilities-memory-corruption-restore-command-patch/ • https://www.zeroday.cloud/blog/redis-cve-2026-25243-deep-dive
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Redis Docker image using docker-entrypoint.sh where redis-server is briefly reparented as PID1 and reaps child helper scripts
  • Operator running `redis-cli --eval` diagnostics on the host that a naive parser mis-attributes to redis-server
  • Backup/monitoring sidecars that wrap redis-server startup in a shell supervisor (parent is the wrapper, not redis-server — verify parent binary)
  • Custom Redis modules that legitimately shell out for maintenance jobs
  • Redis BGSAVE/AOF-rewrite forking a child redis-server (redis-server child, not a shell — excluded by the interpreter allowlist)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker-entrypoint","/usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and grandchildren on the host; a reverse shell, curl|bash, or recon string (id/uname/whoami) confirms RCE. Check redis-server uptime and ACL config for who holds RESTORE/EVAL/XGROUP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the redis-server child tree, and firewall Redis (6379/TLS 6380) from untrusted networks; rotate the requirepass/ACL secrets. 3) Hunt: check the exact Redis branch version against fixed releases (6.2.23/7.2.15/7.4.10/8.2.8/8.4.5/8.6.5/8.8.1), review other Redis nodes for the same parent-shell pattern, and search syslog for redis-server crash/BUG REPORT entries around the same timestamp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "redis-server"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","socat","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "redis-server"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","dash","zsh","ksh","python","perl","socat","ncat","curl","wget") or ActingProcessName endswith "/sh" or ActingProcessName == "sh"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unpatched Redis version exposure to RESTORE-chain RCE (branch-exact) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running Redis builds vulnerable to the July 2026 Streams shared-NACK and RedisBloom/TDigest RESTORE RCE chains by comparing the exact installed version against the per-branch fixed releases (6.2.23/7.2.15/7.4.10/8.2.8/8.4.5/8.6.5/8.8.1). The article stresses checking the exact branch version, not whether Redis was 'recently patched' — 6.2.22 and 7.4.9 were the May destination yet remained exploitable. Rationale: Uses the article's exact fixed-release list per branch to compute vulnerable ranges, catching the four PoC-confirmed builds (6.2.22/7.4.9/8.6.4/8.8.0) plus every other pre-fix build — an inventory-precise, non-generic exposure hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://redis.io/blog/security-advisory-cve202623479-cve202625243-cve-2026-25588-cve202625589-cve-2026-23631/ • https://github.com/berabuddies/redis-poc • https://cybersecuritynews.com/redis-vulnerabilities-enables-rce/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Redis fork/derivative (Valkey, KeyDB, Redis Stack) reporting a Redis-like version string that doesn't map to these branches
  • Air-gapped/internal-only Redis where RESTORE is already ACL-revoked (still shows as vulnerable version but not reachable)
  • Vendor-backported build whose reported version predates the fix but contains the patch (rare, verify with vendor)
  • TVM snapshot lag showing a version already upgraded in the last 24h
  • Development/test containers intentionally pinned to old Redis for regression testing
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName !has "valkey" and SoftwareName !has "keydb"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm the Redis is authenticated-reachable and whether ACL users hold RESTORE (and EVAL/XGROUP, or RedisBloom for 8.8.0); internet-facing + RESTORE-enabled = critical. 2) Contain: as interim mitigation revoke RESTORE from non-essential ACL accounts (`ACL SETUSER ... -restore`) and block untrusted network access to 6379/6380; schedule upgrade to the branch's fixed release. 3) Hunt: pivot flagged hosts into UC1 (redis-server child shell) and UC2 (crash logs) to check whether any were already exploited; expand inventory to Redis running in containers/K8s not covered by endpoint TVM.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "redis"
| extend v = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend major = toint(v[0]), minor = toint(v[1]), patch = toint(v[2])
| where (major==6 and minor==2 and patch<23)
    or (major==7 and minor==2 and patch<15)
    or (major==7 and minor==4 and patch<10)
    or (major==8 and minor==2 and patch<8)
    or (major==8 and minor==4 and patch<5)
    or (major==8 and minor==6 and patch<5)
    or (major==8 and minor==8 and patch<1)
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, EndOfSupportStatus
| order by SoftwareVersion asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-25589", "CVE-2026-25243")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          ParentProcessName

Fake Notepad++ Plugin Delivers MATCHBOIL.V2 in UAC-0099 Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-24 20 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) has warned of a new campaign that involves the use of a malicious program that's dressed up as a Notepad++ plugin to compromise Windows systems. The activity has been attributed by the agency to a threat cluster it tracks as UAC-0099, a Russia-aligned group that has previously observed weaponizing security flaws in WinRAR software to

Exploitation. UAC-0099 fake-PDF VBScript launching Notepad++ / WinRAR (LUNCHPOKE stage) AIDelivery High
Hunts the UAC-0099 loader stage where a VBScript disguised as a PDF (wscript.exe/cscript.exe) directly spawns the bundled legitimate Notepad++ 8.8.3 or WinRAR from an extracted directory. Legitimate Notepad++/WinRAR are effectively never launched by a script host, making this parent→child pair high-fidelity for the initial execution. Rationale: wscript/cscript → notepad++.exe|winrar.exe is a parent/child pair with near-zero legitimate occurrence; the article states the fake-PDF VBS 'extract the contents of the archive and launch Notepad++'. Anchored on named binaries, not a generic script-spawn template. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195923/cyber-warfare-2/uac-0099-is-now-hiding-malware-inside-a-fake-notepad-plugin-to-target-ukrainian-organizations.html
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Software packaging/deployment scripts (SCCM, PDQ) that call winrar.exe from a VBS wrapper
  • Legacy admin logon scripts that launch text editors
  • Custom VBS installers bundled by a helpdesk that unpack with WinRAR
  • Portable-app launchers that shell out to notepad++.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\SCCM\\","\\PDQ","deploy") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Windows\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent VBS path and command line; confirm the .vbs sits in a user-writable/extracted dir (Downloads, %TEMP%, random-named folder) and check whether a decoy PDF opened simultaneously. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the wscript/cscript and child trees, and quarantine the source ZIP/VBS and any Evernote.zip. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for NppExport.dll side-loading, winrar.exe extracting updater.rar, and a scheduled task running RemoteLibUpdater.exe every 3 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VBScript Host Spawning Notepad++ or WinRAR (UAC-0099 LUNCHPOKE)
id: 6f2c1a4e-3b7d-4c1a-9e0f-2a5d8c1b7e40
description: Detects wscript.exe/cscript.exe launching Notepad++ or WinRAR, as seen in the UAC-0099 fake Notepad++ plugin chain.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1059.005
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\notepad++.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\Wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe) @Image:(*\notepad++.exe OR *\Notepad++.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(notepad\+\+|winrar)\.exe$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("notepad++.exe","winrar.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Notepad++ side-loading NppExport.dll from a non-Program Files path (LUNCHPOKE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the DLL side-load core of the UAC-0099 chain: a copy of Notepad++ 8.8.3 running from a randomly-named extracted directory loading a malicious NppExport.dll (LUNCHPOKE) instead of the genuine plugin under Program Files. The pivot is location — legitimate NppExport.dll only ever loads from the installed plugins directory. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious plugin name NppExport.dll plus a location predicate: the genuine plugin only loads from the Program Files Notepad++ plugins folder, so a load from a random extracted directory is the side-load itself. Falcon/Sentinel fall back to notepad++.exe executing outside Program Files since image-load isn't in the provided FDR/Sentinel schema. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-weaponize-notepad-plugins/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable Notepad++ builds run from a USB stick or user profile with a bundled export plugin
  • Developers running a self-compiled Notepad++ from a build/output directory
  • Notepad++ installed per-user under %LOCALAPPDATA% rather than Program Files
  • Software-testing sandboxes that stage Notepad++ in a temp folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Portable","\\Notepad++Portable","\\Dev\\","\\build\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded NppExport.dll and compare to the known-good Notepad++ 8.8.3 plugin hash; inspect its parent directory for winrar.exe, updater.rar and Evernote.zip siblings. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the whole extracted directory (Notepad++ copy + DLL + RAR). 3) Hunt: pivot to any scheduled task launching RemoteLibUpdater.exe and to RemoteLibUpdater.exe loading InitTest.dll.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "notepad++.exe"
| where FileName =~ "NppExport.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\notepad++.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName startswith "C:\\Program Files")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Notepad++ Side-Loading NppExport.dll From Non-Standard Path (UAC-0099)
id: 2b9e7d31-6c48-4f2a-8a1c-5d0f9b3e6a12
description: Detects notepad++.exe loading NppExport.dll from outside the installed Program Files plugins directory, matching UAC-0099 LUNCHPOKE side-loading.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\notepad++.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\NppExport.dll'
  filter_installed:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Program Files\'
      - 'C:\Program Files (x86)\'
  condition: selection and not filter_installed
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 @Image:(*\notepad++.exe OR *\Notepad++.exe) @ImageLoaded:(*\NppExport.dll OR *\nppexport.dll OR *\NPPEXPORT.DLL) -@ImageLoaded:(*\Program Files\* OR *\Program Files (x86)\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\notepad\+\+\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/\\Program Files( \(x86\))?\\/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="notepad++.exe" AND NOT (Processes.process_path IN ("C:\\Program Files\\Notepad++\\*","C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Notepad++\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="notepad++.exe" AND NOT (Processes.process_path IN ("C:\\Program Files\\Notepad++\\*","C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Notepad++\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
WinRAR extracting password-protected updater.rar in UAC-0099 chain AIInstallation High
Hunts LUNCHPOKE unpacking the second-stage payload: the bundled legitimate winrar.exe (or rar.exe) invoked to extract the password-protected updater.rar that contains RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) and InitTest.dll (MATCHBOIL.V2). The archive name updater.rar is a campaign-unique anchor. Rationale: updater.rar is a fixed, campaign-specific archive name named in the article; combining it with the extraction utility yields a very low-noise, article-specific detection for the BURNYBEAR/MATCHBOIL.V2 staging step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-weaponize-notepad-8-8-3/
ATT&CKT1140 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user coincidentally naming a legitimate archive updater.rar (rare)
  • IT distributing a software 'updater.rar' package via WinRAR
  • Backup tooling archiving to a file that happens to match the name
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Windows\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the winrar.exe parent is notepad++.exe or a script host, and that the -p (password) flag or a random destination directory is present; recover the extracted RemoteLibUpdater.exe / InitTest.dll. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine updater.rar and its extracted contents. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for updater.rar drops from EasySend/Evernote.zip lineage and for the 3-minute RemoteLibUpdater.exe scheduled task.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "updater.rar"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where CommandLine has "updater.rar"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR Extracting updater.rar (UAC-0099 BURNYBEAR Staging)
id: 8d41c0a7-72e5-4b19-9f3a-1c7b6e0d2f55
description: Detects winrar.exe/rar.exe extracting the password-protected updater.rar staged by UAC-0099 LUNCHPOKE.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html
  - https://securityaffairs.com/195923/cyber-warfare-2/uac-0099-is-now-hiding-malware-inside-a-fake-notepad-plugin-to-target-ukrainian-organizations.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1140
  - attack.t1560.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'updater.rar'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\winrar.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\unrar.exe) @CommandLine:(*updater.rar* OR *updater.RAR*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/updater\.rar/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")) AND Processes.process="*updater.rar*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")) AND Processes.process="*updater.rar*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Recurring scheduled task running RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR persistence, 3-min cadence) AIInstallation High
Hunts the UAC-0099 persistence mechanism where LUNCHPOKE registers a scheduled task that launches RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) every three minutes. The binary name is campaign-unique and the high execution frequency (many launches/hour, typically via Task Scheduler/svchost) is the distinguishing signal. Rationale: RemoteLibUpdater.exe is a campaign-unique binary named in the article; the >=3 execution threshold captures the article's explicit 'every three minutes' scheduled-task cadence, which no legitimate updater mimics. Sigma omitted because this is a count/threshold aggregation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named internal updater utility coincidentally called RemoteLibUpdater.exe (unlikely)
  • Security tooling repeatedly relaunching a monitored process during testing
  • A crash-loop of a benign service producing many process starts
Suppression filter
| where not (SampleCmd has_any ("\\Program Files\\") and Parents has_any ("services.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate scheduled tasks on the host (schtasks /query or DeviceEvents) for a task pointing at RemoteLibUpdater.exe with a 3-minute trigger; note whether it launches with no arguments (BURNYBEAR resource-exhaustion path) versus loading InitTest.dll. 2) Contain: disable/delete the scheduled task, kill RemoteLibUpdater.exe, isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: correlate to the NppExport.dll side-load and updater.rar extraction, and check for MATCHBOIL.V2 C2 egress from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| summarize Executions=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), FolderPath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, AccountName, SHA256

BURNYBEAR (RemoteLibUpdater.exe) loading MATCHBOIL.V2 InitTest.dll AICommand & Control High
Hunts the final loader hand-off: RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) side-loading InitTest.dll, the modified C#-based MATCHBOIL.V2 loader that fetches secondary payloads. Both the loader binary and the DLL names are campaign-unique, making this a very high-fidelity terminal-stage detection. Rationale: Both RemoteLibUpdater.exe and InitTest.dll are unique names disclosed by CERT-UA/THN; their pairing in a single image-load event is essentially pathognomonic for MATCHBOIL.V2 execution. Falcon/Splunk fall back to the InitTest.dll file drop since image-load isn't in the provided FDR/CIM schema; Sentinel uses the RemoteLibUpdater.exe process-create proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-weaponize-notepad-8-8-3/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate InitTest.dll used by a test harness in a dev environment
  • A security-product module coincidentally sharing the RemoteLibUpdater.exe name
  • EDR-replayed IOC test in a sandbox during purple-team exercises
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitTest.dll and RemoteLibUpdater.exe hashes and the loading directory; check DeviceNetworkEvents from RemoteLibUpdater.exe for MATCHBOIL.V2 C2 or Dropbox WinRAR retrieval. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, delete the 3-minute scheduled task, and quarantine both binaries. 3) Hunt: pivot org-wide on the InitTest.dll/RemoteLibUpdater.exe hashes and on NppExport.dll side-loads to find other compromised hosts.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| where FileName =~ "InitTest.dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

DeviceEvents

Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 21 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian state-supported espionage group spent months reading Western mailboxes through a then-unknown flaw in Zimbra's webmail client. The payload goes after the last 90 days of email, the organization's entire email directory, the password saved in the browser and the codes kept for two-factor recovery. Opening the message was enough to start it. The NSA, CISA and partner agencies published

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ZimReaper C2 & mail exfiltration to actor IPs/domains (TGZ upload + DNS exfil) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call · [LLM] Zimbra Global Address List brute-force via SearchGalRequest two-character enumeration · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ZimReaper CVE-2025-66376 payload staging — DNS to js-*.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua AIExploitation High
Detects the moment the Zimbra Classic-UI stored XSS (CVE-2025-66376) fires and the svg-onload=eval(atob()) stager reaches the actor's payload-staging subdomains. Endpoints that render a booby-trapped webmail message resolve js-<random>.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua from the user's browser process — the earliest on-host evidence of exploitation. Rationale: Anchored on the two named staging subdomains and the fixed '.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua' label pattern (corroborated by Proofpoint/Unit 42). A workstation browser resolving these = ZimReaper stager fetch, i.e. CVE-2025-66376 exploitation firing on render. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal DNS sinkhole / security appliance pre-resolving IOC feed domains for blocking
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox detonation host resolving the domain deliberately
  • Passive DNS / DNS-logging tooling replaying captured queries
  • Researcher validating the IOC on a test host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the endpoint + user; confirm the DNS was browser-initiated (InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser) and that the user runs Zimbra Classic UI. Pull the mailbox and check for an unopened/opened HTML message with fragmented @import + svg onload. 2) Contain: reset the user's Zimbra password, invalidate active webmail sessions, regenerate 2FA scratch codes, and block the domain at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same device/user for GetScratchCodesRequest, CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb', zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE, and any egress to the nine C2 IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".i.zimbrasoft.com.ua"
    or RemoteUrl in~ ("js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua","js-26tik3egye4.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith ".i.zimbrasoft.com.ua"
    or Name in~ ("js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua","js-26tik3egye4.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ZimReaper C2 & mail exfiltration to actor IPs/domains (TGZ upload + DNS exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects endpoints or the Zimbra host communicating with the nine ZimReaper C2 IP addresses or nine actor domains — the channel used to exfiltrate stolen 2FA scratch codes/CSRF token over DNS and to POST 90 days of mailbox contents as a TGZ archive. Straight IOC match on infrastructure confirmed present in both the Unit 42 and Proofpoint indicator lists. Rationale: Uses the nine C2 IPs and nine domains that The Hacker News confirmed appear in BOTH Unit 42's and Proofpoint's indicator lists (shared infrastructure tying CL-STA-1114 to TA488) — high-fidelity IOC match for the mail-TGZ upload and DNS exfil egress. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits

  • Firewall/proxy honeypot or IOC-block appliance beaconing checks against the same IPs
  • 216.252.238.0/24 hosting an unrelated shared service the org legitimately uses (verify the /24 assumption per-hit)
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs actively probing the IPs
  • VPN/NAT egress collapsing many users behind one srcAddr, inflating hits
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal host/user initiated the flow and direction; large outbound bytes to these IPs = probable mailbox TGZ exfil. Check the same host for prior '.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua' DNS. 2) Contain: block all nine IPs and nine domains at perimeter, isolate the involved endpoint, force Zimbra password reset + session invalidation + scratch-code regeneration for the affected mailbox. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host that touched any IOC in 90 days; on the Zimbra server review /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for GetScratchCodesRequest / CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb' / zimbraPrefImapEnabled changes tied to those accounts.

Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on Zimbra SOAP GetScratchCodesRequest (ZimbraAccount namespace) in mailbox/audit logs. ZimReaper's gather_2fa_codes stage calls this API from the hijacked webmail session to pull 2FA recovery codes; Proofpoint states the call 'should be close to absent in normal use', making even a single occurrence high-signal. Rationale: GetScratchCodesRequest is the exact SOAP command name (corroborated by Unit 42's gather_2fa_codes stage description) and is explicitly flagged by Proofpoint as an actionable near-zero-baseline alert — no threshold or correlation needed. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1111 T1539
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine end-user viewing their own 2FA recovery/scratch codes in account settings
  • Zimbra admin auditing a user's MFA configuration
  • Automated backup/migration tooling snapshotting account preferences
  • Penetration-test or MFA-reset support workflow
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the target account and the source session/IP issuing the SOAP call; correlate with recent webmail render of a suspicious HTML message and any '.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua' DNS from the user's endpoint. 2) Contain: immediately reset the account password, invalidate active sessions, and regenerate all 2FA scratch codes (the stolen ones survive a password reset). 3) Hunt: search the same session for CreateAppSpecificPassword 'ZimbraWeb', zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE, and SearchGalRequest bursts; pull the originating message for the fragmented @import/svg-onload pattern with Proofpoint's YARA.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "GetScratchCodesRequest"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a Zimbra app-specific password named 'ZimbraWeb' through the CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest SOAP command. ZimReaper mints this credential to grant IMAP/POP3/SMTP access that bypasses 2FA and survives password resets — the actor's primary persistence mechanism. Rationale: CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest + the literal app name 'ZimbraWeb' are exact strings from the article and Unit 42/Proofpoint; the article's remediation guidance explicitly says to review audit.log for this and delete the ZimbraWeb credential. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/russian-webmail-espionage/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1098 T1556.006
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately creating an app password for a real IMAP/mobile mail client (but rarely named exactly 'ZimbraWeb')
  • Admin provisioning app passwords during a mail-client migration
  • Automation/service account setup requiring app-specific credentials
  • MDM enrollment generating device mail credentials
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the account and whether the user requested any app password; the name 'ZimbraWeb' is the actor's default and is not a normal client name. 2) Contain: delete the ZimbraWeb app-specific password, reset the account password, invalidate sessions, and audit IMAP/POP3/SMTP logins made with it (app passwords survive password resets and skip 2FA). 3) Hunt: check zimbraPrefImapEnabled flips, GetScratchCodesRequest, and outbound IMAP/SMTP from the compromised mailserver to unknown hosts; enumerate all accounts with a ZimbraWeb credential.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest"
    or (SyslogMessage has "CreateAppSpecificPassword" and SyslogMessage has "ZimbraWeb")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled = TRUE) for MFA-free mailbox access AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Zimbra account preference zimbraPrefImapEnabled being set to TRUE, observed by Seqrite in the Ukrainian hydrology-agency case. Combined with the minted app-specific password, this lets the actor pull mail over IMAP without 2FA and persists across password resets. Rationale: zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE is the exact preference/value string from the article's Seqrite January case; the article recommends finding accounts with it set that have no business need for IMAP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1556 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User or admin legitimately enabling IMAP for a desktop/mobile mail client
  • Bulk provisioning enabling IMAP org-wide by policy
  • Mail-client migration turning IMAP on for many accounts
  • Helpdesk enabling IMAP at user request
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference the account against those with a legitimate IMAP business need and against any ZimbraWeb app-password or GetScratchCodesRequest events on the same account. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, set zimbraPrefImapEnabled back to FALSE, revoke app passwords, reset credentials, and review recent IMAP session logins for the account. 3) Hunt: list all accounts recently flipped to IMAP-enabled and correlate with exploitation-time DNS ('.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua') and C2 IP egress; scope which mailboxes had 90-day mail pulled.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "zimbraPrefImapEnabled" and SyslogMessage has "TRUE"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
